question.text:
A portfolio manager is analyzing the performance of a mixed-asset portfolio consisting of 40% equities, 40% bonds, and 20% commodities. The expected return of equities is 10%, bonds is 5%, and commodities is 8%. The standard deviation of equities is 12%, bonds is 6%, and commodities is 10%. The risk-free rate is 3%. The correlations between the asset classes are as follows: equities and bonds: 0.2, equities and commodities: 0.4, bonds and commodities: 0.3.
Which combination of asset classes would potentially reduce the portfolio risk?

explanation.text: The Logic: Equities and Bonds have the lowest pairwise correlation (0.2) among the three pairs, so combining them produces the greatest diversification benefit (greatest reduction in portfolio variance). Equities-Commodities (0.4) and Bonds-Commodities (0.3) are more correlated and offer less risk reduction per unit of weight shift. The Trap: Equities-Commodities tempts because commodities are often pitched as 'diversifiers' — but 0.4 correlation here is higher than equities-bonds. Bonds-Commodities tempts the risk-off candidate. 'All three equally' tempts those who ignore the correlation matrix. The trap is picking based on asset names rather than the actual correlation number. Cross-Exam Context: Correlation-driven diversification is foundational in NISM-Series-X-A, X-B, XV, XXI-B and XIX-C/D/E. Distributor's Pro-Tip: Update your correlation matrix at least annually for PMS clients — 2020-style shocks move historical correlations quickly, and a model-portfolio pitch built on five-year correlations can feel stale when the client sees equity-bond correlation flip positive during a rate cycle.
